title: APD/GBA (Belgium) - DOS-2026-00228
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A company (controller) sent a data subject an email with a formal notice attached to it. The email was sent to the data subject’s work email address, with a third-party email address listed as recipient in the cc field.  
The data subject asked the controller for the identity of the third party. The controller answered that the request would be addressed as soon as possible.  
On another occasion, the controller sent the data subject an email with a payment notice via the data subject’s work email address. Again, the third-party email address was listed as recipient. The data subject asked again for the disclosure of the third party’s identity, and, for an explanation as to where the controller has obtained the data subject’s work email address from. The controller did not respond.  
The controller sent another two emails with a reminder concerning non-compliance with a payment plan and a pre-seizure statement of account to the data subject and, again, to the third-party email address.  
The controller started an internal investigation into the matter and deleted the third-party email address. 
In the course of the communication, amongst other data, the data subject’s name, home address and car licence plate number were revealed to the third party.  
The data subject lodged a complaint with the DPA on the grounds of improper use of their work email address and the disclosure of their personal data to the third-party recipient. Moreover, they requested information regarding the third party involved in their communication, the erasure of their work email address and that none of their personal data be transmitted to the third party.  
The controller demonstrated that the data subject has initiated contact with them via their work email address. The disclosure of the data subject’s data to the third party resulted from an erroneous manual data entry that led to the data subject being associated with the third-party email address in the controller’s debtor record.   
The controller’s failure to respond to the data subject’s request resulted from heavy workload of their employees.  

Holding[edit | edit source]
The decision by the DPA constitutes a prima facie decision as part of the preliminary proceedings prior to the decision on the merits, and not a decision on the merits itself.
As far as the disclosure of the data subject’s data to the third person was concerned, the DPA reminded the controller of their obligation to comply with the principles of data integrity and confidentiality pursuant to Article 5(1)(f) GDPR. Moreover, the controller must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure data integrity and confidentiality (Article 24 GDPR, Article 32(1) GDPR), and to demonstrate accountability (Article 5(2) GDPR). The fact that the third-party email address was linked to the data subject’s communication, and was only removed from the record after the investigation of the controller was launched, which occurred after the data subject notified the controller on several occasions, was not in line with the provisions of the GDPR mentioned above.
When it comes to the controller’s compliance with the data subject’s requests to exercise their rights, the DPA found that the controller’s failure to respond did not appear to be consistent with Article 12(3) GDPR. Under this article, the controller must inform the data subject of measures taken in response to requests pursuant to Article 15 GDPR – Article 22 GDPR. 
As far as the use of the data subject’s work email address is concerned, the data subject initiated contact with the controller via that address, and the controller eventually erased the email address from its system. Therefore, the basis of the complaint has been resolved in that regard, according to the DPA.
The DPA issued a warning pursuant to Article 58(2) GDPR that the controller is likely to violate Article 12(3) GDPR and Article 32 GDPR on the grounds of failure to follow up on the data subject’s request and because the controller revealed the personal data to a third party.

title: NS - 6 As 25/2026-35
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
Two data subjects complained to the DPA about Ceska televize and B.B. (the controller), about the unlawful processing of their personal data. Particularly, the processing operations concerned adults and minors with autism spectrum disorder who had been filmed using a hidden camera for a television programme called Obchod nadeji.
Administrative proceedings were initiated against the controllers by the DPA in 2023, and discontinued by 2025. The data subjects challenged the discontinuation of the proceedings in the Municipal Court in Prague. The Municipal court dismissed the case as a result of a lack of standing, specifically, that the data subjects were not parties to the administrative proceedings and had no right to require a third party to be penalised.
The data subjects argued that Article 78 GDPR gave them the right to effective judicial protection especially since the infringements concerned their personal data. They further emphasised that in denying their request to challenge the discontinuation, breached Article 47 of the European Union Charter of Fundamental Rights and the Czech Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms.
The DPA in return, argued that the proceedings under administrative law, concerned the relationship between the State and the controllers. Furthermore, the DPA emphasised that Czech procedural law governs the standing to challenge decisions in administrative proceedings.
The case made it to the Supreme Administrative Court as an ex officio procedure, to consider whether the data subjects had the right to challenge the decision to discontinue the proceedings concerning third parties. 

Holding[edit | edit source]
The Supreme Administrative Court clarified that data subjects do not have the right to challenge a DPA’s ex officio decision to discontinue administrative proceedings against a third parties. The court restated that the case concerned the relationship between the State and the accused, not the data subject’s individual rights.
Furthermore, the court clarified that whilst Articles 77 and 78 GDPR allow data subjects to challenge decisions regarding their own complaints, and the potential failure of the DPA to respond. However, emphasised that his does not give data subjects the right to demand a third party to be prosecuted in an ex officio procedure.
Therefore, the court dismissed the appeal by the data subjects as they lack legal standing to challenge the decision, upholding the decision of the Municipal Court. However, the court also emphasised that the data subjects retained the right to challenge the decision made by the DPA, regarding their complaint.

title: GHDHA - 200.361.079/01
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The data subject submitted an access request, in electronic format, of his gambling data to Risepoint Limited (the controller), the operator of online gambling services in the Netherlands, pursuant to Article 15 GDPR. This was to allow the data subject to check its accuracy, whether processing was lawful and determine the amounts which were deposited and withdrawn from the service. The controller was willing to provide some data, however refused to provide transaction data, relying on Maltese data protection law.
The data subject brought the issue to court. The Rotterdam District Court ordered the controller, to provide the data subject with his personal gambling data.
The controller appealed on the grounds that the actual intentions behind the data subjects request were so that he could potentially bring a claim against the controller, and that the request was excessive under Article 12(5) GDPR. Furthermore, relying on Maltese data protection law which allows restriction of access in circumstances involving legal proceedings. The controller argued that disclosing the transaction data could affect potential litigation. Finally, the controller claimed that the requested electronic format requested by the data subject was not justified by Article 20 GDPR.
The data subject on the other hand, argued that Article 15 GDPR should entitle him to access his gambling and transaction records as they constituted personal data. The data subject emphasised that a potential legal claim did not invalidate his rights under the GDPR, particularly, right to access. Moreover, the data subject addressed the controller’s reliance on Maltese law, however stated that such must still comply with Article 23 GDPR and satisfy the proportionality and necessity requirements. Finally, the data subject argued that the format requested would allow him to assess the accuracy of his records effectively.


Holding[edit | edit source]
Primarily, the court rejected the controller’s argument that the data subject only made the access request to later bring a claim against them. Relying on the CJEU judgement C-307/22 (FT v DW), the court emphasised that a data subject may request access under Article 15 GDPR for purposes beyond merely understanding the processing operations, such as to establish liability. Thus, the court held that this does not constitute an abuse of their right.
Moreover, the court rejected, the excessive nature of the access request by the data subject argument of the controller. The Court found that in such a context, a request may only be regarded as excessive where objective circumstances demonstrate that the purpose of the access request, pursuant to Article 15 GDPR is not being pursued and that the data subject is clearly manipulating the conditions. The Court found that the controller did not establish such grounds and emphasised that they cannot rely on the burden arising from their business model and large volume of access requests received onto a data subject.
As regards the Maltese data protection law and the restrictions to access, the court rejected the controller’s argument, stating that Article 23 permits certain national restrictions however under the condition that the satisfy the principle of proportionality and necessity. A controller may not simply refuse access because the data may prove useful in legal proceedings, as such would undermine the ability of data subjects to verify the controller’s own records.
Finally, the court found that the data subject’s request to receive his data in an electronically and usable format was valid. The court emphasised Article 12(5) GDPR which requires information to be provided electronically where such a request is made in the same manner. Thus, the court found no reason as to why numerical transaction records could not be given in the format requested.
The controller ultimately incurred the litigation costs of a total of €1,841 which included the filing fee, lawyers’ salary and additional costs.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali (Italy) - 710/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA started an ex officio investigation after IQVIA (the controller) notified a data breach which had been uncovered following the routine inspection of their services. The inspection concerned the collection of personal data from patients from 800 general practitioners (GP) used for observational studied sponsored by pharmaceutical companies. The data breach revealed that the system was able to transfer information entered by GP’s and primary care physicians into free-text fields. This resulted in personal data, capable of identifying patients and doctors, to be found in the controller’s database. Approximately 3,780 patients’ data was affected, of whom 3,080 individuals’ health data was disclosed.
An add-on was installed onto the GP’s software which extracted all information concerning patients and transmitted it to the controller’s database which contained over 1 million individuals’ personal data. This database was construed of longitudinal records which meant that a singular patient could be followed by the use of the persistent patient identifier. Amongst the personal data included therein was diagnoses, prescriptions, medical exams, and other health related data.
During the investigation the controller emphasised that during the extraction process the collected data was anonymised prior to it reaching their database. All directly identifiable personal data points were removed and the patient was assigned a random patient ID. The controller further maintained that it did not have the key necessary to be able to link a patient with the patient ID. It considered the data that it had in its possession to be anonymous and thus not falling within the scope of the GDPR.
Furthermore, it was established that the historical data contained in the controller’s database went back further than 10 years. The controller clarified that data dating back more than 10 years was not processed for research purposes. However, the controller did not provide a procedure for the erasure of such data.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The controller and their obligations 
The DPA held that the contractual agreement and conduct undertaken by the controller clearly demonstrated their role in determining the means and purpose of the personal data processing. The DPA took account of the controller’s ownership of the database, contracts presented, instructions on the extraction and anonymisation of the data and their own use of the database. The DPA therefore held that the controller could not have alleviated itself from its obligations under Article 4(1)(7) and Article 24 GDPR, by merely describing itself as a technological or financial partner. 
Nature of the personal data processed 
As regards the matter of anonymisation, the DPA made reference to the EDPB anonymisation framework, and identified three risks. The DPA held that the Patient ID did not sufficiently counter the risk of re-identification of individuals. Particularly, because even where a patient’s name was not present, a combination with other characteristics in the data set did not necessarily prevent making the individual significantly distinct from others and thus allowed for singling out. 
Furthermore, the DPA found the present case materially different to the CJEU SRB Judgement (C-413/23). In particular, the DPA stressed the necessity for a case-by-case analysis of identifiability and to consider it from the perspective of the entity processing the data. Whilst there was no contention about the general principle underlying the judgment, the DPA held that the controller was not just a passive recipient of pseudonymised data, but rather that they were actively involved in both the processing and anonymisation process. The DPA therefore found it insufficient for the controller to rely on the fact that another party was in possession of the re-identification key.
Legal basis, Information Obligations and Transparency 
The DPA found that the collection and alleged anonymisation (both of which constitute a form of processing requiring a legal basis) by the controller of the personal data of patients was undertaken in absence of an appropriate legal basis. The DPA found a violation of Article 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR. 
The DPA held that whilst there was a contract between the controller and the GP’s, this did not provide a legal basis, as the data subjects, whose personal data was the subject matter, were not part of that contract. Similarly, considering the sensitive nature of the data, even under contractual necessity, the controller would have to identify one of the exceptions under Article 9(2) GDPR, which was not the case. The DPA also found a failure by the controller to provide a legal basis for the anonymisation, which is considered a processing operation. 
Finally, the DPA rejected the controllers claim that the information necessitated by Article 13 GDPR was not provided because the data was anonymous. The DPA found the reliance by the controller on the fact that the GP’s had the obligation to inform was insufficient. The DPA stressed that even the privacy notice did not include all elements required by Article 13 GDPR. 
Principle of storage limitation  
Regardless of the fact that the controller acknowledged the measures taken to comply with the principle of storage limitation, the DPA found that the controller retained historical data yet failed to establish an appropriate procedure for personal data erasure. The DPA held that such storage is inconsistent with the purposes for which the data was being processed and retained beyond the period necessary to achieve those purposes. Therefore, the DPA found a violation of Article 5(1)(e) GDPR. 
The role of general practitioners and processor obligations 
The DPA held that the controller failed to designate the primary care physicians and GPs as processors under Article 28 GDPR, concerning the transmission of their patient’s data to the controller. The DPA found that the GP’s could not have been regarded as controllers of the data as they were not determining the purposes and means of the processing activities.
The data breach and principle of integrity and confidentiality 
The DPA established that in reality, the controller’s software add-on transferred and processed personal data of identifiable indviduals to the controller. This brought about the disclosure and processing of 3,370 patients’ data to SIMG, 3,080 of which included patients’ health data. The DPA found that the controller failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures in violation of both Articles 5(1)(f), and 32 GDPR. 
Principle of accountability and privacy by design 
The DPA further criticised the controller, as there was a lack of evidence suggesting that the controller conducted the necessary analyses to mitigate the risk of re-identification and risks posed by the data collection software to the rights and freedoms of data subjects. The DPA emphasised that the mere implementation of generic technical and organisational measures or reliance on an existing technical solution is insufficient. The DPA found a violation of Article 5(2) GDPR and Article 25 GDPR, the principle of accountability and data protection by design respectively. 
Data Protection Impact Assessment 
The DPA held that the controller violated its obligations under Article 35 GDPR for having initiated the DPIA however failed to complete the processes prior to commencing with its processing operations. The DPA highlighted the nature of data, that is sensitive data, and the clarification by the EDPB in its guidelines for the need to conduct a DPIA for such data. 
In light of its assessment, the DPA found the controller in violation of Articles 5(1)(a), (e), (f) and (2), Article 9, Article 13, Article 25, Article 28, Article 32 and Article 35 GDPR, and imposed a fine of €7,000,000 on them.

title: Tietosuojavaltuutetun toimisto (Finland) - TSV/303/2022
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received a complaint about an online appointment booking service of a healthcare services provider (the controller) in November 2022. According to the complaint, the controller had disclosed personal data of the users of its website (the data subjects) to external tracking service providers.  
A technical report following a DPA investigation into the website revealed that the controller had disclosed data subjects’ therapy appointment booking data and online identification data to Google, Meta, and Microsoft via HTTP requests. The booking data disclosed included information on which type of appointment the user searched for, the therapist selected, and the location of the appointment. The online identification data consisted of technical device identifiers and metadata related to browser functionality, such as device type, screen characteristics, browser version information, and IP address. The data was only disclosed to these recipients if the user had accepted cookies on the website.
The controller stated that it had transferred data to external tracking service providers in accordance with the report. It acknowledged that information concerning appointment scheduling should not have been disclosed to external tracking service providers and pointed out that an error caused by a single employee had led to the extensive disclosure of personal data. However, patient data (such as information on mental health conditions and diagnoses) had only been processed within the controller’s own patient information systems. The controller had subsequently requested the tracking service providers to delete all data they had processed on behalf of the controller through the controller’s website.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA issued the controller a fine of €33,000 for violations of Articles 5(1)(f), 25(1) and (2), as well as 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It also reprimanded the controller for these GDPR infringements. 
First, the DPA held that the data disclosed by the controller contained personal data: it was reasonably possible for Google, Meta, and Microsoft to combine the IP address and device information they received from the controller with their own users’ data and thereby identify users in a situation where users had accepted the use of cookies in their browser and were registered with Google, Meta, or Microsoft services, or had used those services on their devices while logged in. Furthermore, information regarding therapy appointments constituted health data within the meaning of Articles 4(15) and 9 GDPR.
Second, the DPA found that the controller had violated Articles 32(1) and (2) GDPR. According to the DPA, the controller had failed to take into account that the processing involved health data and therefore posed a high risk for the data subjects when implementing technical and organisational measures. In addition, the controller had not used pseudonymisation, anonymisation, or other protective measures before disclosing the personal data to tracking service providers.
Finally, the DPA held that the controller had also infringed the principles of integrity and confidentiality enshrined in Article 5(1)(f) GDPR and failed to meet the requirements for data protection by design and default set forth in Articles 25(1) and (2) GDPR. The DPA noted that a single employee could not be blamed for the failure to comply with the controller's duties. In the same vein, the data subjects' consent to cookies or acceptance of personalised ads could not relieve the controller of its duties under the GDPR.

title: Tietosuojavaltuutetun toimisto (Finland) - TSV/12992/2025
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A user of a social media platform (the data subject) sent the platform (the controller) an email where they objected to the processing of their personal data for direct marketing purposes. The controller replied with instructions on how to delete data stored in the social media app and opt out of targeted marketing in the app's internal settings. 
Following three further emails where the data subject repeated this request, the data subject lodged a complaint against the controller in October 2025. According to the data subject, the controller had violated Articles 12 and 21 GDPR by referring the request to a customer service representative instead of the data protection officer and providing irrelevant and misleading information.
The controller stated that its customer service had provided the data subject information on the basis for targeted advertising, changing advertising settings, deleting data from the app, and how to reduce targeted messages by changing account settings. However, the controller pointed out that it does not target advertising at the data subject at all because the data subject is under 18 years of age and resides in an EEA country. According to the controller, all decisions regarding the purposes and means of processing personal data were made in the United States.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the controller had infringed Article 12(4) GDPR by failing to provide the data subject with a reason for not taking action in response to the data subject’s objection to direct marketing. However, the DPA did not consider it necessary to exercise corrective powers in the case at issue.
First, the DPA held that the GDPR was applicable to the present case as the processing at issue concerned a data subject located in Finland and was related to the offering of social media services to Finnish data subjects.
Second, the DPA pointed out that the controller had not processed the data subject's personal data for direct marketing purposes, as the data subject had been under 18 years of age at the time the request was made. However, the controller's responses had not clearly addressed the data subject's request. The DPA held that the controller should have provided the data subject information on the reason for not acting on the request, i.e. referred to the fact that the data subject’s data was not processed for direct marketing purposes at all.
Finally, the DPA held that the mere fact that the request was answered by a customer service representative rather than the data protection officer did not constitute a GDPR violation. It pointed out that the obligations under Article 12(4) GDPR are generally addressed to the controller, not specifically to the data protection officer.

title: BGH - VI ZR 402/24
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A well-known German singer (the data subject) was secretly photographed by a press photographer while on a walk with her daughter and her mother in the city centre of Munich in May 2022. The photographer sold these images to various news outlets, including Bild, RTL, Freizeitwoche, and Freizeit Revue. Following an unsuccessful warning letter, the defendant was prohibited by a preliminary injunction from displaying or distributing the data subject's images.
The data subject filed a lawsuit against the photographer and claimed at least €10,000 in damages under Article 82(1) GDPR. Alternatively, she based her claim on national provisions, stating the photographer had violated her right of personality.
The court of first instance granted the lawsuit regarding monetary compensation on the grounds of a particularly serious violation of the data subject’s right of personality resulting from the taking and the distribution of the images. Upon appeal by the photographer, the appellate court dismissed the lawsuit. The data subject appealed this decision to the Federal Court of Justice.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The Federal Court of Justice upheld the appellate court’s decision and dismissed the data subject’s appeal. Neither Article 82 GDPR nor the national provisions on the general right of personality could give rise to a claim for monetary compensation in the present case.
The court held that the taking and the disclosure of the images constituted processing of personal data within the meaning of the GDPR. However, these processing operations did not need to be assessed against the substantive requirements of the GDPR – according to the court, they constituted processing for journalistic purposes and fell under the exemption in Article 85(2) GDPR. Consequently, the data subject’s claim for damages could not be based on Article 82(1) GDPR.
The court interpreted the provisions governing data processing for journalistic purposes in its judgment broadly in light of the case law of the CJEU. It could be left open which federal state’s provisions on media privilege were applicable to the photographs at issue, as the taking and the distribution of the images constituted journalism within the meaning of these provisions in any German state. In addition, the court held that responsibility for the editorial content of publications rests solely with the press. A person who provides photographic material to the press is therefore generally not responsible for the content of editorial pieces created on that basis.
Finally, the court concluded that the data subject’s right to her own image and right to privacy were affected by being photographed. However, the freedom of the press and the photographers freedom of occupation outweighed these interests, which precluded a claim for compensation based on the data subject’s right of personality.

title: Datatilsynet (Norway) - 20/03541-37
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The advertising technology company Xandr (controller, at that time AppNexus, now a part of Microsoft) engaged in so-called real-time bidding. Real-time bidding is a technology where advertisers can bid against each other via an automated process to show their personalised advert to a user of a website or app. It occurs every time a user visits a website or app where there is an available ad space.  
Within this auction process, Xandr acted both on the buyer and seller side, meaning it provided both a supply side platform and a demand side platform. It offered to its clients a console, a tool to interact with its platform, where the clients were able to conduct, optimize and track their advertising transactions. Through the platform, Xandr receives ad requests of their clients and enriches the bid with information which segment(s) a user belongs to. The bid request is sent to advertisers who evaluate the request and decide whether to bid on the ad space. Real-time bidding requires the collection, accumulation and dissemination of personal data to target and personalise the advertisement and optimise the bid. The console offers settings where the clients of Xandr can exclude certain categories of data from bid requests or to exclude certain recipients from receiving bid requests.  
Within this process of real-time bidding at hand, Xandr processed personal data of Grindr users in Norway. Grindr is a dating app with a target market in the LGBTQ+ community. Amongst the data processed by Xandr was the information that individuals were using Grindr, their advertising ID, and IP addresses. This data was shared with third-party advertisers. 
On the one side, Xandr provided assistance to Grindr to make its ad spaces available to potential buyers. On the other side, Xandr also operated on the demand side and send ad requests to third parties where an ad should be placed on the Grindr app, through an intermediary that had access controls within the console. 
The Norwegian Consumer Council lodged a complaint with the DPA on the basis of Article 80(1) GDPR. An additional complaint was filed regarding GDPR violations by Grindr. 


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA found a violation of Article 6(1) GDPR and Article 9(1) GDPR.
The DPA held that the personal data processed (app name, app ID and app URL) were personal data pursuant to Article 4(1) GDPR. This is true for online identifiers that can make a natural person identifiable. 
As far as the role of Xandr as controller was concerned, the DPA held that Xandr acted as joint controller pursuant to Article 26(1) GDPR because it made decisions on the purposes and means of processing. While a processor may make certain decisions on the purposes and means, decisions of essential means are reserved to the controller. Joint controllership is assumed when the processing would not be possible without both parties’ participation in the purposes and means. 
When Xandr acted as advertiser and its platform placed ad buying bids to display ads on the Grindr app, it acted as joint controller with Grindr. In this process, ad buyers select a “segment” for a particular ad campaign. Xandr made available standard segments that the ad buyers could chose from. Therefore, according to the DPA, Xandr influenced the processing. 
When Xandr’s platform processed ad delivery and bid requests originating from Grindr, it acted partly as controller and partly as processor. Xandr maintained that it assumed the role of processor of Grindr, which is an assessment that is not supported by Grindr. The DPA considered that Xandr pursued its own objective of being a facilitator of exchanges between publishers and advertisers that involves data processing on its multi-sided platform. It was Xandr that defined the infrastructure and constraints for those exchanges. Xandr had an interest both when it came to the number of participants in that exchange system as well as when providing precise marketing and maximising value for advertisers and publishers were concerned. An aspect of that was the procedure of enrichening ad requests for ad spaces on the side of Xandr, which benefits Xandr and Grindr likewise. While Grindr was able to control categories of data contained in bid requests as well as the recipients thereof through the console offered by Xandr, it was on Xandr’s side to provide the framework for exercising such control, for example by deciding what advertisers Grindr was able to interact with. In case Grindr did not make any selections within the console, the standard settings decided on by Xandr would apply and the bid request would be circulated to the recipients that Xandr included on its platform. By providing the framework and offering its service on the console with the standard selected by Xandr, Xandr had a tangible impact on the determination of the purposes and means of processing. Moreover, Xandr could instruct Grindr on the categories of data shared with it.
The DPA recurred to the broad understanding of the concept of “controller” according to CJEU case law and took into consideration the opaque practices in the AdTech industry where a large number of companies exchange personal data along complex value chains. It is unlikely in this ecosystem that one actor alone fully controls how the data is processed. According to the DPA, a failure to hold these companies accountable would result in diffusion or elimination of responsibility, also with regard to data subjects’ rights. This would run counter the objective of the GDPR to ensure a high level of data protection. The fact that neither Xandr nor Grindr accepted controllership would result in an evasion of responsibility to answer to data subjects’ rights. However, the notion of controller is a functional concept that is determined by factual circumstances and not by contractual agreements. Since both Xandr and Grindr pursued their respective interests and purposes when processing the personal data, they both exercised decisive influence on the decision on the means of processing. The processing could not have taken place without the contribution of both parties in deciding the purposes and means, making them joint controllers.
While joint controllers may distribute tasks and divide responsibility pursuant to Article 26(1) GDPR, the accountability principle (Article 5(2) GDPR) as well as the obligations under Article 24 GDPR apply to both controllers. Compliance cannot be outsourced and both controllers are responsible and must demonstrate compliance with the GDPR, for example when it comes to determining a legal basis for the processing.
The DPA found that Xandr processed special categories of personal data pursuant to Article 9(1) GDPR. The information that a person is being registered on Grindr is to be considered information about someone’s sexual orientation.  
In the separate Grindr case before the DPA, the DPA found that the information that data subjects were Grindr users was not “manifestly made public” by the data subjects pursuant to Article 9(2)(e) GDPR. Xandr could also not rely on explicit consent pursuant to Article 9(2)(a) GDPR. It never obtained the consent directly from the data subjects itself. The consent that Grindr obtained from its users did not fulfil the requirements of Article 4(11) GDPR and Article 7 GDPR. Therefore, it was invalid. 
Both joint controllers must have a valid legal basis for the processing. The fact that Grindr was responsible for collecting the data subjects’ consent did not exempt Xandr from its accountability obligations under Article 5(2) GDPR and Article 24 GDPR. Despite the fact that it is possible to contractually oblige one joint controller to collect consent on behalf of the other, the other controller must ensure that the consent meets the requirements of Article 4(11) GDPR and Article 7 GDPR. Since the data at hand concerned special categories of data, Xandr was not able to discharge of its accountability obligations simply by contractual agreement. It did not take any additional measures to ensure that the consent given was lawful. Therefore, Xandr breached Article 9(1) GDPR.
When it comes to the legal basis of Article 6(1) GDPR when processing personal data of Grindr users, since the consent that Grindr collected was invalid and Xandr did not provide sufficient information as to the legal basis, no legal basis was applicable. Therefore, the DPA found a violation of Article 6(1) GDPR.
The DPA fined Xandr NOK 92 m (€8.5 m). When it comes to the reasons for issuing the fine, the DPA argued that with Article 6(1) GDPR and Article 9 GDPR, Xandr violated core data protection rights of individuals and basic requirements for processing personal data. The intransparency of the AdTech ecosystem was found an aggravating factor. Moreover, the data subjects did not initiate the processing and did not intend to share their personal data with Xandr and its 4,000 advertising partners for commercial purposes. The nature of the personal data affected, namely data on sexual orientation, was taken into account as well as the fact that Xandr financially benefitted from the unlawful processing. 
The fact that the procedure is, according to Xandr, an industry practice, cannot be considered a mitigating factor. This fact only reinforces the need for an administrative fine with a deterrent effect.
The DPA held that Xandr acted negligently because Xandr is a leading advertiser technology company and the processing of personal data on a large scale is a core part of its business. Therefore, it can be expected of Xandr to be acquainted and compliant with central data protection requirements. It was negligent of Xandr not to make any assessments regarding the lawfulness of the processing.   
The amount of fine pursuant to Article 83(5)(a) GDPR was based on Xandr’s revenue, not on Microsoft’s because for the time period concerned, Xandr was not a part of Microsoft yet.

title: OLG Köln - 15 U 340/25
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A rapper (the data subject) requested the operators of a search engine (the defendants) to delist a search result in March 2022. When the data subject’s name and the word “Nazi” were entered in the search engine, the search results referred to an article about a person who was allegedly deeply involved in the neo-Nazi scene. The article contained a picture that suggested this person had managed the sales booth for the data subject’s fashion label at an event. 
The defendants refused to remove the search result. Following this, the data subject filed an action for injunctive relief requesting the search result to be delisted. The defendants blocked the search results after a witness had stated in a hearing before the court of first instance that the person mentioned in the article had nothing to do with managing the data subject’s sales booth. 
The court of first instance granted the injunction under Article 17(1)(d) GDPR in the territory of the Federal Republic of Germany. It held that the processing had been unlawful as the statement about the defendant having a business relationship with a person involved in neo-Nazi circles was found to be untrue. 
The defendants appealed this decision to the Higher Regional Court of Cologne. The data subject also appealed the decision as they found the court had wrongly limited the claim for injunctive relief to German territory.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The court granted the defendants’ appeal and dismissed the data subject’s appeal. It held that the data subject had no right to an injunction under Article 17(1)(d) GDPR.
According to the court, a legally enforceable claim for erasure and supplementary injunctive relief against a search engine operator to have a search result delisted exists only if the search engine operator has violated its duty to review the content based on a request from the data subject. Otherwise, the search engine operator is not liable for the display of search results that refer to unlawful content. In the present case, the defendants had not violated such duties:  they were not required to recognise that the information in the article was untrue until this was confirmed by the witness in the hearing before the court of first instance.
In addition, the court held that the data subject must provide the search engine operator with sufficient and relevant evidence proving that the information contained in the search results is manifestly inaccurate if they dispute the accuracy of the search results. 
A mere assertion and the presentation of evidence during litigation are generally insufficient. As the data subject had simply asserted that the person with neo-Nazi connections had not managed their sales booth, the processing at issue had been necessary for exercising right of freedom of expression and information within the meaning of Article 17(3)(a) GDPR.

title: BAC (Bulgaria) - 2984/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The data subject requested that the controller (a Bulgarian non-banking financial institution specialized in providing online fast loans and installment loans) provide copies of all documents containing their personal data, including loan agreements, credit applications, and information about payments made under their contracts. The controller provided only an extract from its records and information about the processing of the data, without supplying copies of the requested documents.
The Administrative Court of the city of Lovech annulled the controller's refusal and ordered the company to reconsider the request in accordance with the law. It held that the company had failed to fulfil the individual’s right of access to personal data under Article 15 of the GDPR.
The controller appealed to the Bulgarian Supreme Administrative Court (BSAC), arguing that the lower court’s decision was inadmissible or legally incorrect. The company also requested that the proceedings be suspended pending a related case before the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), Case C-676/2025.
The BSAC rejected the request to suspend the proceedings, finding that the pending CJEU case concerned different circumstances, namely contractual relationships that had already ended. Since the contractual relationship in the present case had not been shown to have ended, the outcome of the CJEU case was not decisive. The Court also confirmed that the controller's response constituted an explicit refusal because it did not provide the requested document copies in the first place.
The BSAC confirmed that Article 15(3) GDPR requires a data controller to provide a copy of the personal data being processed, including data contained in stored documents. Referring to the CJEU judgment of 4 May 2023 in Case C-487/2021, it explained that this right may require copies of entire documents, rather than extracts alone, where necessary for the individual to understand and verify the accuracy and lawfulness of the processing of their data. Loan agreements, repayment schedules, credit applications, and related financial information may all contain personal data covered by this right.
The BSAC clarified that access may be restricted to protect the rights and freedoms of third parties according to [[Article 23 GDPR#1]] GDPR. The controller had therefore to take care not to disclose personal data belonging to other individuals contained in the requested documents. However, no other applicable grounds for restricting access were established in this case.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The Court noted that Article [[Article 23 GDPR]] establishes certain restrictions on the right of access to personal data. Since the controller had not invoked national security, defence, public security, or any of the other grounds for restriction listed in Article 23(1)(a)–(h) and (j), the only relevant limitation in this case was Article 23(1)(i), concerning the rights and freedoms of others. Accordingly, the controller had to protect the personal data of third parties and must not disclose personal data relating to other individuals if such data appears in the requested documents. This limitation did not, however, justify withholding the applicant’s own personal data contained in the requested documents.
The BSAC therefore upheld the finding that the controller had failed to comply fully with its obligations under [[Article 15 GDPR]] by providing only an extract from its records instead of the requested document copies, subject to the necessary protection of third-party rights.

title: BVwG - W292 2301903-1
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The data subject was an existing customer of a telecommunications provider (the controller).
An unknown third party used the data subject’s name, date of birth and bank account number to order a mobile phone contract and smartphone through the controller’s online shop without the data subject’s knowledge and provided a delivery address that had no connection to the data subject.
The controller did not verify the identity of the person placing the order or compare the delivery address with the data subject’s existing address information. Despite instruction to require identity verification for the delivery, the delivery company handed the package to an unknown third party and recorded the data subject as the recipient.
The data subject lodged a complaint with the Austrian Data Protection Authority (DPA), alleging that the controller had allowed a third party to use their personal data to conclude a contract without adequate identity verification.
The controller argued that it had selected personal delivery with an identity check as an appropriate security measure. It also argued that the delivery company was independently responsible for the failure to check the recipient’s identity.
The DPA upheld the complaint. The controller appealed to the Austrian Federal Administrative Court.

Holding[edit | edit source]
First, the court held that the controller had violated Article 5(f) GDPR, Article 24 GDPR and Article 32 GDPR by failing to implement adequate technical and organisational measures to prevent identity fraud.
Second, the court held that the controller had violated Article 5(1)(d) GDPR, which requires controllers to ensure the accuracy of personal data. By failing to verify the data subject’s identity or check the delivery address against the information already held for this existing customer, the controller had failed to take adequate measures to ensure data accuracy.
Third, the court rejected the controller’s argument that arranging personal delivery with an identity check was sufficient. The controller had not convincingly explained how it monitored compliance with the personal delivery requirement. Relying on the delivery company’s contractual obligation to verify the recipient’s identity did not affect the controller’s own obligations.
Finally, the court upheld the DPA's finding that the controller had infringed the data subject’s right to confidentiality under § 1 DSG, read together with Article 5(1)(d) GDPR, Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, Article 24 GDPR and Article 32 GDPR. It dismissed the appeal and held that a further appeal was inadmissible.

title: Datatilsynet (Denmark) - 2025-31-2078
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received a complaint from a former employee (data subject) of the controller concerning the refusal of an access request. More specifically, the data subject was dismissed by the controller on the basis of having gained access to the data subjects’ correspondence with another employee on Messenger. The data subject therefore requested access to the material on which the employer had based the decision.
The controller clarified that the correspondence which was the basis of its decision to refuse access was discovered by chance on another employees work phone when they had turned it in following their resignation. The controller further emphasised that it took into consideration the criminal proceedings that had been initiated concerning the access of the correspondence. Particularly the fundamental need to safeguard the controller’s legal position in light of those proceedings.
The data subject on the other hand argued that whilst refusal to an access request is allowed this should not result in refusal to all personal data and information of the data subject. The data subject also argued unlawful obtention of the correspondence by the controller and the corresponding compelling interests of the data subject as a result thereof, to be provided with a copy of the information. Finally, the data subject emphasised the fact that controller did not provide specific information as to the grounds for refusal. That being clear identification of which rights and freedoms would be violated if the data subject had obtained a copy, and the compelling public interest which outweighs those of the data subject.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the controller acted within the limits of its right to refuse an access request in accordance with Article 15(4) GDPR, where the data subject’s interests are outweighed by compelling private and public interests. In this regard, as a result of the material to which the data subject had requested access was also the subject of criminal proceedings, the DPA found that such constitutes a private and public interest. 
Nonetheless, the DPA found that the rejection response provided by the controller to the data subject was not sufficiently comprehensive and substantiated as required by Article 12(4) GDPR. The DPA held that the response by the controller was phrased very generically without making reference to the specific circumstances and interests taken into account when determining to refuse access. 
Therefore, whilst the DPA found the controller to be in compliance with its right to reject an access request, it further held that the controller failed to provide the data subject with an adequate explanation regarding the decision to refuse access. As a result, the DPA issued a reprimand against the controller.

title: AEPD (Spain) - PS/00194/2025
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received notification from Vodafone Espana S.A.U. (the controller) about a data breach which resulted in unauthorised access to the processors infrastructure. This caused the confidentiality and availability of the personal data stored on the servers linked to the controller’s incident response service, to be compromised. This breach affected 486,786 residential customers and 14,571 enterprise customers unencrypted personal data.
Throughout the investigation, it was found that the breach on the processors systems occurred as a result of the exploitation of a critical vulnerability. Importantly, the vulnerability was discovered in January 2023 and assigned a critical severity rating. Nonetheless, the processor took any action to implement measures ensuring that the security of the personal data is being safeguarded from any attacks. This directly contributed to the cyberattack and data breach which occurred later in May 2023.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that in light of the vulnerability being discovered months before the occurrence of the data breach, the controller failed to ensure that its data processor provides sufficient guarantees through the implementation of technical and organisational measures to ensure the security of their systems. Particularly, the DPA criticised the lack of periodic audits and checks done by the controller, which would have allowed for early detection and action to mitigate against the vulnerability.
The DPA considered this a failure by the controller to implement measures which contributed to the materialisation of a foreseeable and avoidable risk. Therefore, the DPA found the controller in violation of Article 32 GDPR and imposed a fine of €400,000 taking into account the number of affected individuals the negligent nature of the incident and certain aggravating factors.

title: AEPD (Spain) - PS-00028-2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received a data breach notification from the Spanish Cycling Federation (the controller), after a technical error allowed a legitimate user to manipulate the browser URL and access other user’s data. The breach affected the confidentiality and integrity of 261,965 minors and adults’ personal data. This included names, date of birth, videos and pictures, identification documents and contact information. The DPA subsequently received three complaints concerning the data breach.
During its investigation, it was clarified that the incident had a duration of at least two months, however that the controller had taken technical precautions after detecting the increased server errors. The controller had blocked IP addresses associated with the mass inquiries made on the platform. Regardless, server logs which were reviewed at a later stage revealed the breach.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the controller was obliged to ensure that personal data is being processed with appropriate security to mitigate against the risk of unauthorised or unlawful processing.
The DPA found that whilst the controller had the basic security controls, they were inadequate in practice. The DPA emphasised the inadequate access controls, the absence of multifactor authentication, the insufficient early detection, weakness in data retention and the lack of evidence proving they have taken steps to improve the situation.
Ultimately, the DPA found the controller in violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR. Taking into account the number and categories of affected individuals, the types of personal data, negligent nature of the breach and aggravating factors, the DPA imposed a fine of €4,800 on the controller. This fine was imposed under the conditions that recognises its responsibility, voluntarily pays the penalty and waives administrative appeals against the decision.

title: HDPA (Greece) - 18/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The complainant, an electrical engineer, submitted a complaint to the Hellenic DPA on 26-03-2024 after the Decentralized Administration of the Aegean refused her requests to remove her name from eleven administrative decisions published on the Diavgeia portal (open-government platform that publishes official public sector decisions and expenditures online). These decisions concerned the rejection of applications submitted by third parties for drilling and water-use permits, where the complainant acted as an authorized representative or engineer.
According to the complaint:
-The published decisions explicitly identified the complainant by name and referred to her role as the authorized representative of the applicants.
-The decisions stated that requested supporting documents had not been submitted and that no response had been received from the authorized representative or the applicants within the prescribed deadlines.
-The complainant argued that she had never consented to the publication of her personal data and that the wording of the decisions created the false impression that the permit applications were rejected because of her professional inadequacy, thereby harming her professional reputation.
-On 24-05-2023 and through subsequent requests, she exercised her right to erasure and requested the removal of her name from the published decisions. The Administration rejected those requests, maintaining that publication was legally required by the legislation governing Diavgeia and that the GDPR right to erasure did not apply.
During the DPA proceedings, the Administration argued that the publication served the objective of public-sector transparency and that the complainant's name was necessary for adequately explaining the reasons for rejecting the permit applications.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The Hellenic DPA held that the publication of the complainant's personal data in the eleven decisions was unlawful.
According to Article 76(3)(k) of Law 4727/2020, only individual administrative acts whose publication is expressly required by a specific legal provision may be uploaded to Diavgeia. The Administration relied on Article 4(10) of Joint Ministerial Decision 146896/2014, which requires publication of decisions granting water-use and water-resource permits. However, the Authority found that this provision applies only to granted permits and not to decisions refusing permit applications. Therefore, the eleven rejection decisions were not legally required to be published on Diavgeia.
As a result, the Administration could not rely on Article 6(1)(c) GDPR (processing necessary for compliance with a legal obligation), and the publication lacked a valid legal basis. The Authority therefore found a violation of the principle of lawfulness under Article 5(1)(a) GDPR and Article 6(1)(c) GDPR. 
The DPA further held that the Administration unlawfully refused the complainant's erasure requests. Since the processing itself was unlawful and the Administration failed to demonstrate any exception under Article 17(3) GDPR, it should have removed the complainant's name from the decisions or otherwise anonymized the information. Its failure to do so constituted a violation of Article 17(1)(d) GDPR.
Consequently, the Hellenic DPA:
-Imposed a €2,000 administrative fine on the Decentralized Administration of the Aegean for violating Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1)(c) GDPR;
-Issued a reprimand for violating Article 17(1)(d) GDPR;
-Ordered the Administration to immediately remove the eleven decisions from Diavgeia and report compliance to the Authority within 20 days.
